title: Introduction to B+ Tree
description: The B-tree variant that keeps all data in linked leaves, ideal for range queries

sections.title: 2. What Makes a B+ Tree Different
3. Internal Nodes as a Pure Index
12. Pitfalls and How to Think About It

blocks.text: A B+ tree is a refinement of the B-tree that has become the standard structure for database indexes and file systems. It keeps the same wide, shallow, balanced shape, but changes where the data lives.
In a B+ tree, all the actual records sit in the leaf nodes, and the leaves are linked together in a chain. The internal nodes hold only copies of keys that act as signposts for searching.

blocks.caption: A B+ tree keeps data in linked leaves, with internal nodes acting as an index
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655269-773719985.png

By the end of this topic you will understand exactly how a B+ tree differs from a B-tree, why the linked leaves make range queries so fast, and why nearly every relational database chooses it for indexing. It is the B-tree, tuned for the queries databases actually run.
If a B-tree is a great general purpose disk structure, the B+ tree is that same structure tuned for the one thing databases do most: scanning ranges of sorted data quickly and predictably.
To appreciate the B+ tree, recall the B-tree it builds on. A B-tree is a wide, shallow, self balancing search tree, designed to minimise slow disk reads by packing many keys into each node.
In a plain B-tree, every node, internal or leaf, stores both keys and their associated data. A search can therefore finish early if it finds its key in an internal node near the top.

items: A B-tree is wide and shallow to reduce disk reads
Keys are kept sorted within each node
Both internal and leaf nodes store real data
It stays balanced through splitting and merging

blocks.text: The B+ tree keeps all of these strengths, then reorganises where data is stored to make ordered access dramatically better.
The one detail to hold onto from the B-tree is that it mixes data into every node. That single choice is what the B+ tree changes, and almost every difference flows from it.

Everything good about a B-tree, its shallowness, its balance, and its low disk read count, carries straight over to the B+ tree. The B+ tree only reorganises where data sits, keeping every one of those strengths.

content.title: 2. What Makes a B+ Tree Different

blocks.text: The defining change is simple to state: in a B+ tree, data lives only in the leaves. The internal nodes carry no records at all, only keys used for routing.

blocks.caption: A B-tree stores data everywhere; a B+ tree stores data only in the leaves
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655270-946800841.png
blocks.alt: What Makes a B+ Tree Different

blocks.text: Because records are only in the leaves, every search must travel all the way down to a leaf. There is no early exit at an internal node like there can be in a B-tree.

This might sound like a downside, but it buys two big advantages: the internal nodes become smaller and can hold more routing keys, and the leaves can be linked together to make ordered scans trivial.

items: Records are stored only in leaf nodes
Internal nodes hold only keys, no data
Every lookup descends fully to a leaf
Smaller internal nodes mean an even shallower tree

blocks.text: Concretely, imagine looking up a key that happens to be a signpost in the root. In a B-tree you might find its record right there and stop. In a B+ tree that root entry is only a pointer, so you keep descending until you reach the leaf that actually holds the record.

The trade you are making:

You give up the occasional early exit, and in return you get smaller internal nodes and a linked leaf level. For database workloads that trade pays off enormously.

content.title: 3. Internal Nodes as a Pure Index

blocks.text: In a B+ tree the internal nodes form a pure index. Their keys are signposts that tell the search which child to follow, and the same key value can appear both as a signpost above and as a real record in a leaf.

blocks.caption: Internal nodes only route the search; the real records all live in the leaves
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655270-18763446.png
blocks.alt: Internal Nodes as a Pure Index

blocks.text: Because internal nodes store only keys and child pointers, and no bulky records, each one fits more routing keys into the same disk block. More keys per internal node means more children per node, which makes the tree even shorter than an equivalent B-tree.

Duplication is intentional:

A key can appear as a signpost in an internal node and again as a stored record in a leaf. This small redundancy is what lets the internal levels stay a lean, fast index.

Because the index carries no records, more of the tree total size sits in the leaves and less in the internal levels. The internal index becomes a thin, fast map that often stays cached in memory even when the leaves live on disk.

items: Internal nodes store keys and child pointers only
No records means more keys fit per node
More keys per node means more children and fewer levels
The lean index often stays cached even when leaves are on disk

blocks.text: The second signature feature is that all the leaves are linked together in a doubly or singly linked list, in sorted order from smallest to largest.

blocks.caption: The leaves form a sorted linked list for fast sequential scans
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655270-144412973.png

This chain turns the bottom level of the tree into a sorted sequence of every key in the structure. Once you reach any leaf, you can walk left or right through neighbouring leaves without going back up through the tree.
That single design choice is what makes range queries and ordered traversals so efficient, as we will see next. It is the main reason databases prefer B+ trees.

Picture the leaves as pages of a book laid end to end. The internal nodes are the table of contents that jumps you to a page, and the next pointers let you simply turn to the following page without consulting the contents again.

items: The leaves together hold every key in sorted order
Each leaf points to the next leaf, and often the previous one too
Reaching one leaf gives instant access to its neighbours
This is the foundation of fast ordered scans

blocks.text: A search routes down through the internal nodes exactly like a B-tree, but it never stops until it reaches a leaf, because that is the only place records live.
At each internal node you find the child whose range contains your key and follow it. When you arrive at a leaf, you look for the key among the records stored there.

codes.python:
def search_leaf(node, key):
    while not node.leaf:
        i = 0
        while i < len(node.keys) and key >= node.keys[i]:   # routing
            i += 1
        node = node.children[i]
    return node   # the record, if present, is in this leaf

blocks.text: Every search costs the same, the full height of the tree, which makes performance uniform and predictable. Databases value that consistency.

Trace a lookup for 25 in a tree whose root signposts are 20 and 40. Since 25 is between 20 and 40, you follow the middle child, and continue until a leaf, where you finally check whether 25 is actually stored.
The upside of always reaching a leaf is uniformity: every lookup costs the same number of steps, so query times are steady and easy to reason about, which databases prize.
This is where the B+ tree truly shines. A range query asks for all keys between a low and a high bound, and the B+ tree answers it beautifully.

blocks.caption: Descend once to the start of the range, then walk the leaf chain until you pass the end
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655271-159376983.png
You descend once to the leaf holding the low bound, then simply walk the linked leaf list collecting keys until you pass the high bound. There is no repeated traversal from the root for each item.
The cost is one descent plus a linear walk over just the results. A plain B-tree, lacking the leaf chain, would have to do a full in order traversal, which is far more work.

Compare the two structures on a query for everything between 15 and 45. The B+ tree descends once to 15 then strolls along the leaf chain to 45. A plain B-tree must instead perform a full in order traversal, repeatedly climbing and descending, to visit the same keys in order.

items: Descend once to the leaf containing the lower bound
Scan forward through that leaf collecting matches
Follow the next pointer to continue into the following leaf
Stop as soon as a key exceeds the upper bound

blocks.text: Insertion works like a B-tree, but with one twist tied to the leaves. You descend to the correct leaf and add the key in sorted order.

blocks.caption: When a leaf splits, its first key is copied upward as a signpost
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655271-180750624.png

If the leaf overflows, it splits into two leaves, and the two are joined into the leaf chain. Crucially, when a leaf splits, the smallest key of the new leaf is copied up to the parent as a signpost, while the key itself remains in the leaf.

This differs from a B-tree, where a split moves the median key up and out of the node. In a B+ tree the key stays in the leaf so that all data remains at the leaf level, and only a copy goes up to guide searches.

items: Descend to the leaf and insert the key in order
If the leaf overflows, split it and link the new leaf into the chain
Copy the new leaf smallest key up as a routing signpost
Internal splits push a key up as usual, and a root split adds a level

blocks.text: The copy up rule is the detail people forget. In a B-tree the median leaves the node and moves up; in a B+ tree a copy of the boundary key goes up while the original stays in the leaf, because leaves must hold every record.
Internal node overflow behaves just like a B-tree: the node splits and a key rises to its parent, possibly cascading up to a new root. Only the leaf level uses the special copy up rule.
Deletion also parallels the B-tree, with the leaf list kept consistent. You remove the key from its leaf, and if that leaf falls below the minimum, you repair it.

Repair means borrowing a key from an adjacent leaf that has spare keys, or merging with a neighbouring leaf when neither sibling can spare one. When leaves merge, the chain pointers are updated so the linked list stays intact.

items: Remove the key from its leaf
If the leaf is underfull, borrow from a sibling leaf
Otherwise merge with a sibling and fix the leaf chain
Update the internal signposts to match the new leaf boundaries

blocks.text:
Keep the chain honest:

Any split or merge at the leaf level must update the next pointers. A broken leaf chain silently ruins range queries, so it is a common source of bugs.

As with a B-tree, deletions that leave a node healthy need no repair at all. Only when a leaf dips below its minimum do you borrow or merge, and even then the fix is local to a couple of neighbouring leaves.

items: Remove the key from its leaf
Borrow from a neighbouring leaf if it has spare keys
Otherwise merge two leaves and relink the chain
Adjust the internal signposts to match the new leaf boundaries

blocks.text: Given the choice between a B-tree and a B+ tree, real databases almost always pick the B+ tree, for several concrete reasons.

items: Range queries and ordered scans are extremely fast thanks to the leaf chain
Internal nodes hold only keys, so they fit more children and the tree is shallower
Every lookup costs the same, giving predictable performance
Sequential access, common in reports and scans, walks the leaves directly

blocks.text: Since databases constantly run queries like give me all orders between two dates, the leaf chain is worth far more than the occasional early exit a plain B-tree offers.

Think about a report that asks for every transaction in a given month. That is a range query, and the B+ tree answers it by touching only the relevant leaves in order, which is exactly the access pattern databases optimise for.
This is why, when you add an index to a column in a relational database, the engine almost always builds a B+ tree rather than a plain B-tree behind the scenes.
The B+ tree matches the B-tree on the core operations and beats it on ordered access.

items: Search: O(log n), always descending to a leaf
Insertion and deletion: O(log n), including any splits or merges
Range query: O(log n) to find the start, then linear in the number of results
Space: O(n), with a little duplication of keys as signposts

blocks.text: That range query bound is the headline. Finding a contiguous slice of sorted data costs only the descent plus the size of the answer, which is essentially optimal.

Where it wins:

On single key lookups a B+ tree and a B-tree are both logarithmic. On range and ordered scans the B+ tree is in a different league, thanks to the linked leaves.
Placing the two side by side makes the trade off clear.

blocks.caption: Choose a B+ tree for range scans and uniform lookups, a B-tree for possible early hits
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406655271-97452536.png

items: B-tree: data in every node, so a lucky lookup can stop high in the tree
B+ tree: data only in leaves, so every lookup reaches the bottom
B-tree: no leaf chain, so range scans need a full traversal
B+ tree: linked leaves make range scans and ordered iteration trivial

blocks.text: For general ordered storage on disk, especially with range queries, the B+ tree is the clear winner, which is why it dominates database indexing.

In short, a B-tree can occasionally answer a point lookup faster, but a B+ tree answers range and ordered queries far faster and offers steadier, more predictable performance. For databases, the second set of properties matters much more.

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Think About It

blocks.text: When you reason about B+ trees, keep a few things front of mind.

items: Remember that data lives only in the leaves; internal keys are just signposts
On a split, a leaf key is copied up, not moved up as in a B-tree
The leaf chain must be maintained on every split and merge
Reach for a B+ tree whenever range queries or ordered scans matter

blocks.text:
The mental model:

Picture a fast index on top and a sorted linked list of all records at the bottom. The index finds your starting point; the linked leaves let you read forward as far as you like.
A frequent interview trap is to describe a B-tree split when asked about a B+ tree. Be precise: leaf splits copy a key up and keep it below, and the leaf chain must always be relinked.
The B+ tree is the workhorse index of the database world, and for good reason.

items: It is a B-tree variant that stores all data in the leaves
Internal nodes are a pure key index, so the tree is very shallow
The leaves are linked, making range queries and ordered scans fast
All operations are O(log n), and range queries add only the result size
It is the standard structure for database indexes and file systems

blocks.text: Whenever you run a range query on an indexed column, picture the B+ tree descending once and then gliding along its linked leaves to gather the answer.
If you carry one picture away, let it be a slim index sitting above a long sorted linked list of leaves: jump in through the index, then read forward through the leaves as far as the query needs.
